body.text: Two US-based academics who reframed the thinking of John Maynard Keynes after the oil crises of the 1970s won the Nobel Prize in Economics.

Robert E. Hall of Stanford University and Michael Woodford of Columbia University will share the 12 million-krona ($1.2 million) award for their work on the “microeconomic foundations of macroeconomic stabilisation”, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences in Stockholm said in a statement on October 12.
“The laureates have helped us smooth out the economy’s peaks and troughs,” the academy said in a statement.

Hall is affiliated with Stanford University in California, and Woodford with Columbia University in New York. Woodford spoke to the committee by phone on October 12 from New York, saying: “It’s a tremendous honour; it’s a surprise.” Hall was praised for a 1978 article on how consumers prefer consumption to stay stable, while Woodford then developed the so-called New Keynesian model that has since proven highly influential among global policymakers to this day.

“The laureates’ work has provided us with a stable theoretical foundation for the models that are now used by central banks and governments around the world,” John Hassler, chair of the prize committee, said in a statement. “With them, we are better equipped to deal with shocks in the economy, such as energy crises or sudden changes in how much households consume.”

“Rather than basing the models on statistical links between macroeconomic variables, such as inflation, production, and consumption, they chose to build them on a microeconomic foundation,” the academy jury said. “This encompasses an understanding for how the total mass of individual households and businesses affect the economy through their actions.”

The economics prize is formally known as the Bank of Sweden Prize in Economic Sciences in Memory of Alfred Nobel. Last year, the economics award went to American-Israeli Joel Mokyr, France’s Philippe Aghion, and Canada’s Peter Howitt for research into how technology drives and affects growth.

Woodford was asked if any economic event or shock had ensured that his new framework had really stood up to the test. He cited how central banks adapted their toolkit to the global financial crisis of 2008 as they confronted a slump in demand that reductions in borrowing costs on their own could not solve.

“Forward guidance about policy, so making more explicit statements about the likely future path of interest rate policy as opposed to relying on simply being able to cut interest rates further immediately—that was an important part of the policy response,” he said. “It did contribute to better stabilisation. It didn’t magically solve the problem, but I think it was an important contribution.”
Hall studied consumer decisions
Hall studied the way that consumers’ decisions about whether and how much to spend depend on what they expect their future income to be.

“If they are optimistic, they will consume more than if they are pessimistic,’’ the committee wrote. But consumer expectations can change unexpectedly as new information about the economy comes in. And some households are so poor they can’t borrow or tap savings in response to economic changes.

In a 1982 paper with the economist Fredric Mishkin, Hall found that around 80 per cent of households made spending decisions based on their expectations for the future “while the rest lived hand to mouth”, the committee wrote.
Woodford analysed how businesses make decisions

Woodford’s research established that businesses make decisions about prices based on where they think interest rates will go in the future. “If the business believes that its competitors’ prices and its own costs will increase, it is best to set a higher price than it would with the opposite expectation,” the Nobel committee wrote. “Businesses’ decisions are thus also governed by their expectations.’’

Therefore, central banks such as the US Federal Reserve, which set short-term interest rates, should provide “clear and credible communication about how they reason and what they plan to do”. Central banks have responded to this insight by working harder to explain what they are doing.
During the phone call broadcast at the news conference, Woodford said his work has stressed “the understanding of the people who are in the markets and making decisions about spending”.

The money for winners this year was increased by 1 million kronor per category in connection with the 125th anniversary of the awards. When the first Nobel Prizes were given out in 1901, the amount was 1,50,782 kronor each.

The Economics Prize is the only Nobel not among the original five created in the will of Swedish scientist Alfred Nobel. It was created instead through a donation from the Swedish central bank in 1968, leading detractors to dub it “a false Nobel”. But like the Nobels in Chemistry and Physics, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences chooses the winner and follows the same selection process.

Last week, South African judge Navi Pillay won the peace prize, and Canadian-Icelandic writer Anne Carson was named the literature laureate. The Nobel Prize in Chemistry was awarded to Frenchman Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai of Japan, and the Physics Prize to Belgian Francis Halzen. And the first prize to be announced, in medicine, went to American Karl Deisseroth and Germans Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel. Like the other Nobels, the economics prize consists of a diploma, a gold medal, and a $1.2 million cheque. The laureates will receive their prizes at formal ceremonies on December 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death in 1896.
(With inputs from agencies)
